Account for signal handling in job control and traps: when job control is disabled, commands in an asynchronous list inherit an ignored action for SIGINT and SIGQUIT, and a trap for a signal received while the shell waits for a foreground command runs only after that command completes.

Name trap conditions portably: use EXIT (or 0) and symbolic signal names without the SIG prefix rather than numbers (numeric signal conditions are guaranteed only on XSI systems), and do not attempt to trap SIGKILL or SIGSTOP because doing so is undefined and has no effect.

Quote trap actions to control expansion timing: each action is processed like eval when the trap fires, so a single-quoted action defers expansion and trap "eval \" $cmd\"" runs a variable command safely, whereas an unquoted $cmd breaks on special characters; also know the EXIT-trap environment equals the state after the last command, invalid signal names are not syntax errors, and traps persist until changed.

Account for trap inheritance limits: signals ignored on entry to a non-interactive shell cannot be trapped or reset, entering a subshell resets non-ignored traps to their defaults, trap with no operands lists current traps in a form suitable for saving and restoring, and the ERR trap is a non-portable KornShell extension.

Protect background jobs from SIGHUP with 'disown' or 'disown -h', remembering Bash exits on SIGHUP and an interactive shell forwards it to its jobs, and that huponexit sends SIGHUP to jobs when an interactive login shell exits.
Remove a job from the active jobs table with 'disown', or keep it running while shielding it from SIGHUP with 'disown -h'.

Use '--' to end option processing on most builtins so dash-leading data is not misread as options, remembering the exceptions (':', true, false, test/'[' ignore '--', and exit/return/break/continue/let/shift accept dash-leading arguments), and that builtins run inside the shell process.
For POSIX-style tools, place the end-of-options delimiter before user-provided operands so dash-prefixed input is not parsed as another option.
Protect operands from unintended shell or option parsing by using --, ./ prefixes, quoting, escaping, or explicit dotfiles as the situation requires.

Run '. file' (source) to execute a file's commands in the current shell rather than a subshell (so its variable and function definitions persist), searching PATH and, outside POSIX mode, the current directory, without needing the execute bit.
Remember that a redirection with no command name is performed in a subshell, so use the exec special built-in when a file-descriptor change must persist in the current shell environment.

Use the dot utility to run a file in the current shell environment, knowing it is located through PATH (and need not be executable) and deliberately does not search the current directory unless PATH permits, which is a guard against trojan-horse scripts.
Pass positional parameters to a sourced file as arguments to '.', knowing the caller's positional parameters are left unchanged when none are supplied.
Break out of or continue an outer loop with 'break n' or 'continue n' (n at least 1).
Use break, continue, endless loops, select, and until only when their termination and validation behavior remains explicit.

Parse options with 'getopts optstring name' (which sets name, OPTIND, and OPTARG), always resetting OPTIND to 1 before re-parsing a new argument set in the same shell because it is not reset automatically, and prefix optstring with ':' for silent error handling.
Test whether a shell option is enabled with '[[ -o optname ]]'.
Parse shell-script options with getopts and shift processed options so each option and remaining argument has a clear handler.
Parse command invocations as command name, options, and arguments, with case-sensitive options and conventional short, long, and clustered forms.
Implement option parsing with either manual loop-case-shift logic or getopts, choosing based on long-option needs and clustered short-option support.
Run 'hash -r' (or reassign PATH) after installing or moving an executable, since Bash caches command locations and would otherwise use the stale path.
Account for 'test'/'[' comparing '<' and '>' by ASCII outside POSIX mode but by the current locale in POSIX mode or within '[['.
Set the file-creation mask with 'umask', reading its octal digits as subtracted from 7 (so a umask of 022 yields 755 permissions).

Bind a shell command to a key sequence with 'bind -x keyseq:command', which exposes the line as READLINE_LINE and the cursor and mark as READLINE_POINT and READLINE_MARK and reflects changes to them in the editing state.

Command-line editing is provided by Readline (enabled by default interactively unless --noediting, Emacs bindings by default, switchable with 'set -o vi'), configured through ~/.inputrc (named by INPUTRC) or the 'bind' builtin.
Produce a stack trace with 'caller [expr]', which reports the line number, subroutine name, and source file of an active call frame.
Build stack traces from the parallel call-stack arrays FUNCNAME, BASH_SOURCE, and BASH_LINENO (FUNCNAME[0] is the current function and the bottom element is 'main'), which the 'caller' builtin uses.
Report the current line number with LINENO, for example in error and debug messages.
Disable a builtin with 'enable -n name' so a same-named external command runs instead, and load a dynamically-loadable builtin with 'enable -f filename name'.

Prefer 'printf' for reliable formatted output: the format is reused until all arguments are consumed (missing ones treated as empty or zero), '-v var' stores the result instead of printing, '%q' quotes a value for safe reuse as shell input, and '%(datefmt)T' formats times.
Use printf rather than echo for script-grade formatted output, and treat format/argument mismatches as bugs.

Control 'read' with its options: -a to fill an array, -d for a custom delimiter, -n/-N for a fixed number of characters, -s to suppress echo, -p for a prompt, -u to read from a descriptor, and -t for a timeout (which returns a status above 128 and applies only to terminals, pipes, or special files).
Read user input into descriptive variables and choose silent, fixed-width, or delimiter-limited modes only when the prompt semantics require them.
Use read safely with prompts, raw mode, silent mode, timeouts, defaults, IFS control, and here strings according to the input source and sensitivity.
Set resource limits with 'ulimit' (-H hard, -S soft; a non-root user cannot raise a hard limit once set, and specifying neither sets both).
Enable 'set -u' (nounset) to turn a reference to an unset variable into an error, remembering the exceptions for the special parameters '@' and '*' and arrays subscripted by '@' or '*'.
Use set -u (nounset) to catch references to unset variables (the @ and * special parameters are deliberately exempt) and set -n (noexec) to parse a script for syntax errors without executing it.
Apply 'set -P' to make directory-changing commands use the physical structure without resolving symlinks, and 'set -m' (monitor) to enable job control with separate process groups.

Rely on privileged mode ('set -p', applied automatically when the effective and real user ids differ) ignoring BASH_ENV/ENV, environment-imported functions, and the SHELLOPTS/BASHOPTS/CDPATH/GLOBIGNORE environment variables, which is the security default for setuid contexts.

Expect Bash started with the effective and real ids differing and without '-p' to read no startup files, ignore environment-imported functions and the SHELLOPTS/BASHOPTS/CDPATH/GLOBIGNORE environment variables, and reset the effective id to the real id.

Handle environment-sensitive shell variables carefully: ENV is expanded and sourced only for interactive shells and is ignored when real and effective user or group IDs differ, assigning PWD can make cd and pwd unspecified, environment-initialized variables are auto-exported, and changing LC_CTYPE does not affect the running shell lexing.
Branch on effective user ID when a script must behave differently for privileged and unprivileged users.

Tune optional behavior with 'shopt -s'/'-u' (options are off by default, '-q' reports state via exit status), for example histappend (append rather than overwrite history), checkhash (re-verify a hashed command exists), and localvar_inherit (a new local inherits an outer same-named variable's value and attributes).
Never leave an empty element in PATH (as '::' or a leading or trailing colon), because a null element means the current directory and lets a malicious file there be executed as a command.

Introspect execution with BASH_COMMAND (the current or about-to-run command, useful in DEBUG and ERR traps), BASH_SUBSHELL (the subshell nesting depth, 0 at top level), and '$_' (the previous command's last argument).
Use the readonly EUID for a trustworthy privilege (for example root) check, since it cannot be overwritten by an attacker-controlled assignment.
Use superuser powers sparingly, prefer sudo where available, exit elevated shells promptly, and verify effective identity before privileged changes.
Use RANDOM for reproducible pseudo-random integers (0-32767, seedable by assignment), and SRANDOM for a non-seedable 32-bit value from a strong source when unpredictability actually matters.
Read wall-clock time from EPOCHSECONDS (whole seconds) or EPOCHREALTIME (floating-point microseconds) instead of shelling out to 'date'.

Account for startup environment variables that reconfigure the shell: POSIXLY_CORRECT enters POSIX mode before startup files, and the readonly SHELLOPTS and BASHOPTS enable their listed options at startup and propagate to exported child shells.

Place configuration in the right startup file: an interactive login shell reads /etc/profile then the first of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, or ~/.profile; an interactive non-login shell reads ~/.bashrc (so ~/.bash_profile commonly sources ~/.bashrc); and under the name 'sh' Bash enters POSIX mode and reads only the file named by ENV.
Control filename-expansion ordering with GLOBSORT (name, numeric, size, mtime, atime, ctime, or blocks, with '-' to reverse or 'nosort' for filesystem order) rather than post-sorting glob results.

Know the filename-expansion rules: a slash and a leading period in a name must be matched explicitly (so globs neither cross directory separators nor reveal dotfiles by default), matching requires read permission on directories with pattern components and search permission on the rest, results are sorted by the current locale, and a pattern that matches nothing is left unchanged.
Exclude non-executable files such as shared libraries from PATH command search and completion with EXECIGNORE patterns, which do not affect the test, '[', or '[[' commands.
Separate execution-trace output from program output by pointing BASH_XTRACEFD at a dedicated file descriptor when using 'set -x'.
Use xargs when pipeline output must become command arguments, and preview or trace commands before destructive execution.
Gate features on the Bash version using BASH_VERSION (a string) or the readonly BASH_VERSINFO array (major, minor, patch, build, release-status, machine-type).
Use Bash internal state and formatting features to avoid external commands, while preserving fallbacks, version gates, and randomness warnings.
Unset HISTFILE (or set it null) to stop the shell from persisting command history, which matters when handling sensitive commands.

Understand history handling: it is enabled by default interactively ('set -o history'), keeps HISTSIZE entries in memory (stored after history expansion), reads and writes HISTFILE (default ~/.bash_history; histappend to append; HISTFILESIZE to cap; nothing saved when HISTFILE is null), and is filtered by HISTIGNORE and HISTCONTROL.
Measure elapsed wall-clock time cheaply with SECONDS, assigning to it to reset the baseline.
Set TMOUT to a positive value to time out 'read' and 'select' on terminal input and to auto-logout an idle interactive shell as a hardening measure.
Use Bash read timeouts as a sleep replacement only on supported Bash versions, and reuse a descriptor for high-frequency sleeps.

Invoke Bash with the set single-character options plus multi-character options first: '-c string' runs a command string (extra arguments become $0 then the positional parameters), '-l' a login shell, '-i' interactive, '-s' reads standard input, '-r' restricted, and '--' ends options so following arguments are a script and its arguments.

Distinguish a login shell (argv[0] beginning with '-' or invoked with --login) from an interactive shell (no non-option arguments unless -s, no -c, standard input and error both terminals, or started with -i) when reasoning about which files run.
Detect an interactive shell inside a startup script by testing whether '$-' contains 'i' or whether PS1 is set (it is unset in non-interactive shells).

Do not treat interactive testing as proof a script is robust, because an interactive shell survives nounset and '${var:?}' expansion errors, builtin redirection errors, a failed 'exec', a special-builtin error, and parser syntax errors that would terminate a non-interactive script.

Do integer arithmetic aware that it uses the largest fixed-width integers with no overflow check (division by zero is an error), that variables may be referenced by bare name (a null or unset one being 0), and that a leading 0 makes a constant octal, 0x makes it hex, and 'base#n' sets an arbitrary base.

Use indexed arrays (zero-based integer subscripts, auto-created by 'name[i]=value' or declared with 'declare -a') and associative arrays (arbitrary string keys, declared with 'declare -A'), which have no size limit and need not be contiguous.
Assign arrays with the compound form 'name=(value ...)', supplying explicit non-empty subscripts (or alternating key/value pairs) for associative arrays.

Reference an array element as '${name[subscript]}' (braces required) and iterate an array with '"${name[@]}"', which yields each element as a separate quoted word and nothing when the array is empty, reserving '"${name[*]}"' for a single IFS-joined string.
Get an array's element count with '${#name[@]}' and a single element's length with '${#name[subscript]}'.
Never reference an array variable without a subscript expecting the whole array, because a bare '$name' is equivalent to '${name[0]}' and yields only the first element.
Use a negative index on an indexed array to count back from the end, where -1 references the last element.
Manage recently-visited directories with the directory stack builtins 'pushd', 'popd', and 'dirs', where the current directory is always the top of the stack.

Build prompt strings (PS0, PS1, PS2, PS4) from backslash escapes such as \u, \h, \w, \$, and \[ ... \] to bracket non-printing terminal sequences, and be aware the decoded prompt is further subjected to parameter expansion, command substitution, and arithmetic expansion (under promptvars), which can trigger unintended expansion if the text contains special characters.
Design the prompt as a compact status display with safe PS1 syntax and clear separators around dynamic fields.

Treat a restricted shell (rbash, --restricted, or -r) as only a partial control - it blocks cd, changing PATH/SHELL/HISTFILE/ENV/BASH_ENV, slash-containing command or source names, output redirection, 'exec', importing environment functions or SHELLOPTS, and disabling itself - but its limits apply only after startup files and an executed script runs unrestricted, so pair it with a locked-down PATH, a non-writable working directory, and a cleaned environment.
Prefer operating-system mechanisms such as jails, zones, or containers over a restricted shell when a genuinely secure restricted environment is required.
Keep shared shell configuration source-only, centrally tracked, generic across shell families, and guarded for interactive use.

Use the shell compatibility level (the BASH_COMPAT variable, or legacy compatNN options) only as a temporary migration aid with a single level active, and rely on current Bash resetting loop state on function and subshell entry so 'break' or 'continue' does not leak into the caller's loops.
Rely on Bash not forking a subshell when a control structure such as an 'if' or 'while' is redirected, so variables assigned inside a redirected loop persist in the current shell.

Reference jobs with a jobspec - '%n' by number, '%string' by command prefix, '%?string' by command-line substring, '%%'/'%+'/'%' for the current job, and '%-' for the previous - noting a bare '%1' means 'fg %1' and '%1 &' means 'bg %1', and an ambiguous match is an error.
Stop a foreground job with the suspend character (typically Control-Z) and then use 'bg', 'fg', or 'kill', or force a stop by sending SIGSTOP.
Resume a job with 'bg' to continue it in the background or 'fg' to bring it to the foreground and make it the current job.
Suspend the current shell with 'suspend' until it receives SIGCONT, supplying '-f' to override the block on a login shell or one without job control.

Account for Bash deferring job-status notifications until the next prompt (unless 'set -b'), removing a terminated job from the table after notifying (while 'wait' with its PID still reports the status), and warning once before an exit that would terminate stopped jobs.

Wait for children with 'wait [id]' (returns the last id's status, or waits for all background jobs with no arguments), 'wait -n' for whichever finishes next (127 if none is a child, pairing with 'wait -p varname'), and 'wait -f' to wait for actual termination rather than a state change.
In non-interactive scripts, where job control is inactive, give 'kill' and 'wait' process ids rather than jobspecs, which they do not accept there.
List jobs with 'jobs', using '-l' to add process ids, '-p' for only the process-group-leader id, and '-r' or '-s' to restrict to running or stopped jobs.
Send a signal to a job or process id with 'kill' (SIGTERM by default, accepting a case-insensitive name with or without the SIG prefix or a number), and list or map signals with 'kill -l'.
Choose the line-editing mode with 'editing-mode' in the inputrc or 'set -o emacs'/'set -o vi'; in vi mode a new line starts in insert mode and ESC enters command mode (k/j move through history).
Edit a long or multi-line command in an editor with C-x C-e (edit-and-execute-command), which invokes $VISUAL, then $EDITOR, then emacs and executes the result.
Use vi modes and basic insert, write, quit, undo, delete, yank, paste, and join commands to make controlled text edits.
Bind keys in an inputrc as 'keyname: function-name' (no space before the colon), a quoted string for a macro, or '"keyseq": function' using Emacs-style escapes such as \C-, \M-, and \e.
Branch inputrc settings with the conditional directives '$if' (testing mode=, term=, version, the application name, or a variable), '$else', '$endif', and '$include file'.

Enable helpful Readline toggles such as completion-ignore-case and show-all-if-ambiguous, and keep enable-bracketed-paste on so pasted text is inserted literally rather than executing editing commands bound to sequences within the paste.

Use the default Emacs editing keys - C-a/C-e (line start/end), C-k/C-u (kill to end/start), C-w (kill previous word), C-y (yank), M-./M-_ (insert the previous command's last argument) - and C-r/C-s for incremental reverse/forward history search.
Insert a literal control character or Tab with C-v or C-q (quoted-insert), and stash a command into history without running it with M-# (insert-comment).
Rely on TAB completion trying programmable completions for the command word first, then variable, username, hostname, or command completion, and finally filename completion.

Define argument completion with the 'complete' builtin (a compspec; -E for an empty line, -I for the initial word, -D as the default), and in a '-F function' place matches in the COMPREPLY array using $1 (command), $2 (word being completed), $3 (preceding word), and the COMP_WORDS/COMP_CWORD/COMP_LINE/COMP_POINT variables.

Generate completions from the appropriate source (-C command, -W wordlist, -G glob pattern, -F function; -X to filter, -P/-S to add a prefix or suffix) and shape behavior with '-o' options such as filenames, nospace, nosort, and the bashdefault/default/dirnames/plusdirs fallbacks.
Load completions lazily by returning exit status 124 from a completion function after installing the real compspec, the pattern the bash_completion dynamic loader uses.
Generate matches with 'compgen' inside a completion function and adjust the active completion's options on the fly with 'compopt'.
Manage the history list with the 'history' builtin - '-c' to clear, '-d' to delete, and '-a'/'-n'/'-r'/'-w' to append, read, or overwrite the file for sharing history across sessions.
Re-run or edit past commands with 'fc' ('fc -s pat=rep' for a substitution re-run, commonly aliased as 'r'), whose editor is chosen by ${FCEDIT:-${EDITOR:-vi}}.
Use vi search, substitution ranges, global replacement, and confirmation flags to make targeted edits instead of manual repeated changes.
Choose bash command-line editing mode deliberately and persist vi-style editing only when it matches the user workflow.

Never let a quoted string or a backquote command substitution begin in one context and end in another, because a backquote substitution or quoted string that straddles a double-quote boundary produces undefined results.

Treat reserved words as recognized only when unquoted and in specific grammatical positions, quote a word to stop it being taken as a reserved word, and avoid [[ ]], function, and select as portable keywords because their recognition is implementation-defined.
Do not depend on a #! interpreter line for POSIX portability, because the standard leaves the result unspecified when a shell input file begins with #!.

Distinguish a variable that is set to null from one that is unset (a null value still counts as set and is cleared only by unset), and enclose any positional-parameter number with more than one digit in braces such as ${10}.

Double-quote a parameter expansion to suppress field splitting and pathname expansion on its result, and choose the ${parameter:-}, :=, :?, or :+ form deliberately, minding that the colon variants test for unset-or-null while the colon-less variants test only for unset.

Expect each field to undergo pathname (glob) expansion after field splitting unless set -f is in effect, so quote a value or enable set -f (noglob) to keep literal characters such as * and ? from matching filenames.

Choose the modifying parameter-expansion form for intent: ${parameter:=word} assigns a default (variables only, never positional or special parameters), ${parameter:?word} fails fast by writing to standard error and exiting non-zero when the value is missing, and ${parameter:+word} substitutes only when the value is present.

Control here-document expansion by quoting the delimiter: an unquoted delimiter expands the body for parameter, command, and arithmetic expansion (with backslash behaving as inside double-quotes) while quoting any part of the delimiter word suppresses all body expansion; also use <<- to strip leading tabs and do not assume the here-document descriptor is seekable.
Use here documents for multi-line embedded input or output, choosing quoted delimiters, escaping, and tab-stripping behavior to match expansion and indentation needs.

Account for interactivity in error handling: a non-interactive shell exits on a syntax, expansion, variable-assignment, special-built-in, or special-built-in redirection error while an interactive shell does not, an error in a special built-in is more fatal than one in an ordinary utility, and an error in a subshell exits only that subshell before execution continues in the caller.

Treat special built-ins as more privileged than ordinary utilities: an error in one may abort the shell, they need not be reachable through the exec family of functions, and those not conforming to the Utility Syntax Guidelines do not accept a -- argument.

Model a simple command as: save the words that are variable assignments or redirections, expand the remaining words so the first field is the command name, perform the redirections, then expand and apply the variable assignments; and note that when no command name results the assignments affect the current environment.
Use export to give variables the export attribute so their values appear in the environment of subsequently executed commands, and use name=word to set the value at the same time.

Handle non-executable targets defensively: an ENOEXEC failure makes the shell re-run the file as a shell script (returning 126 and an error for a non-text file), and executing any standard utility with standard input not open for reading or standard output/error not open for writing yields a non-conforming environment.

Do not assume && binds tighter than ||: the two operators have equal precedence and left associativity, so an AND-OR list evaluates strictly left to right and needs explicit grouping when a different grouping is intended.

Treat a backgrounded command specially: a semicolon or newline sequences a list while an ampersand runs it asynchronously in a subshell without waiting, the exit status of an asynchronous list is always zero regardless of outcome, and the special parameter $! holds the process ID of the last command of the most recent background list.

Choose the grouping construct by the environment you need: ( compound-list ) runs in an isolated subshell so its assignments and directory or option changes do not persist, whereas { compound-list; } runs in the current environment; separate two leading parentheses with white space so a subshell group is not mistaken for arithmetic evaluation, and terminate the brace group closing } with a control operator.

Rely on the defined loop and conditional semantics: a for loop skips its body when the item list is empty and defaults an omitted in-list to "$@", while and until loops iterate on a zero or non-zero condition status respectively, an if runs the matching then or else branch, and each construct exit status is that of the last body command executed or zero if none ran.

Use case for first-match dispatch: the word is expanded and compared against each pattern in order using shell pattern-matching notation, only the first matching branch runs, and the exit status is zero when no pattern matches.

Account for two tokenizer subtleties: a quoted word is never recognized as a reserved word (quoting a keyword forces it to be a plain word), and a word is treated as a variable assignment only when the characters before the first unquoted equals-sign form a valid name, so a token beginning with an equals-sign is not an assignment.

Expect a trapped signal received while the shell waits on the wait utility to make wait return immediately with a status greater than 128 before the trap runs, and do not depend on any particular order when several trapped signals are pending because that order is unspecified.

Pass state to child utilities only through exported variables: a utility that is not a special built-in runs in a separate environment seeded from the parent that receives only exported variables, it does not change the shell environment unless its own description says so (as cd and umask do), and a shell-script utility has the shell caught traps reset to default.

Treat a subshell as an isolated duplicate: it copies the environment but resets non-ignored traps to their defaults and its changes never propagate back to the parent, and command substitutions, parenthesized groups, asynchronous lists, and each stage of a multi-command pipeline all run in subshells, so state set there does not survive.

Scope break and continue carefully: they act on the nth enclosing loop (default 1, capped at the outermost) and only when the command is lexically enclosed by the loop in the same execution environment, so driving them from a function body, a sourced script, or a trap can produce unspecified behaviour.

Treat eval as a second round of shell parsing: it concatenates its arguments with spaces and re-reads and executes the result, returns zero for no or only-null arguments, and because it need not honour --, guard arguments that might begin with a hyphen (for example by prefixing a space) and never eval untrusted input.
Use eval only for genuinely dynamic commands, and build the evaluated string from validated fragments to avoid injection.

Use exec by mode: with no command it applies redirections to the current shell so opened descriptors persist (close descriptors above 2 explicitly since they may otherwise leak into invoked utilities), and with a command it replaces the shell without creating a new process, returning 127, 126, or 1-125 on failure.

Know the set output and option syntax: set with no options or arguments lists all variables re-inputtably, options are enabled with a hyphen and disabled with a plus-sign, set -o prints option state in an unspecified format, and set +o prints it in a form suitable for re-input to restore the same options.

Manage positional parameters through set with care: giving arguments unsets all existing positional parameters before assigning the new ones, a lone hyphen as the first argument is unspecified, and set -- both delimits arguments that could start with a hyphen or plus (as in set -- "$x") and, with no further arguments, unsets all positional parameters.

Reach for the diagnostic and safety options as needed: set -x traces each expanded command to standard error, set -v echoes input as read, set -C (noclobber) protects existing files from > (overridable per file with >|), set -f (noglob) disables pathname expansion, set -h remembers a function utilities at definition time, and set -m runs jobs in their own process groups.
